name: DiskANN
question: What if the index doesn’t fit in memory?
summary: DiskANN, from Microsoft Research, stores a graph index (Vamana) and full-precision vectors on SSD and keeps only compressed vectors in RAM. The search walks the graph using the compressed codes, reads a handful of SSD pages per query, then re-ranks with full vectors. It serves billion-scale datasets from a single machine with modest RAM.
useCases: Hundreds of millions to billions of vectors
RAM costs that make in-memory HNSW impractical
Latency targets in milliseconds, not microseconds

items.detail: a single-layer graph with long-range edges; few hops per query
a few page reads per query
exact distances on full vectors at the end

steps: Consider it when vectors × bytes exceeds the RAM you can afford
Use fast NVMe SSDs, since latency depends on random reads
Tune the search list size and beam width for recall versus I/O
Benchmark p95 latency under concurrent load, not single queries
pitfalls: Slower than in-memory HNSW at small scale
Index builds for very large datasets take a long time
Performance depends heavily on SSD quality
remember: Graph on SSD, compressed copy in RAM.
caption: 1B × 768 × 4 bytes ≈ 3.1 TB in RAM versus 1B × 32 bytes = 32 GB of codes.

code.text: data=vecs, distance_metric="l2",   # unit vectors: L2 ranks like cosine
graph_degree=64,                   # R: max edges per node in the Vamana graph
complexity=100,                    # candidate list size while building
search_memory_maximum=32.0,        # GB of RAM at search: sets PQ code size, ~32 B each
num_nodes_to_cache=500_000)    # hot nodes near the entry
complexity=100,  # L: candidate list, recall vs SSD reads
beam_width=4)    # SSD reads issued per round trip
# Results are ordered by exact distances from the full vectors already read

steps.title: Size the problem
steps.text: 1 billion × 768 dims × 4 bytes ≈ 3.1 TB, far beyond one server's RAM. Compressed PQ codes of 32 bytes each need only 32 GB.

steps.title: Build a Vamana graph
steps.text: One flat graph with at most R = 64 edges per node. Its pruning keeps some long-range edges, so a search needs few hops.

steps.title: Split storage between SSD and RAM
steps.text: Each node's full vector and neighbour list sit together in one 4 KB SSD sector. RAM holds only the PQ codes, plus a cache of hot nodes.

steps.title: Start at the entry point
steps.text: Every search begins at a fixed medoid. Cached nodes around it are served from RAM, which saves the first SSD reads.

steps.title: Beam search over the SSD
steps.text: Each round reads the best unvisited candidates by PQ distance, beam_width = 4 at a time. With L = 100 that is about 25 round trips.

steps.title: Re-rank with the full vectors
steps.text: The sectors already read contain full-precision vectors, so exact distances order the final 10 with no extra I/O.

pros: Billion-scale search from a single machine
RAM needs fall by an order of magnitude or more
Full vectors on SSD give exact re-ranking without extra reads
cons: Latency depends on SSD random-read performance
Very long builds for large datasets
Slower than in-memory HNSW when data fits in RAM
Fewer managed options and tuning guides
avoidWhen: The data fits comfortably in RAM (HNSW is faster and simpler)
Only network-attached or spinning disks are available

playgroundGuide.scenario: An image-search service in Bengaluru holds about a billion embeddings and has one server with 256 GB of RAM and local NVMe SSDs. Use this sizing tool to decide whether an in-memory index is possible and, if not, how to configure DiskANN. Sizes are exact arithmetic; recall and latency come from a simple model.
controls: Drag the vector count and pick dimensions and PQ code size.
Drag the candidate list L and pick a beam width.
Pick the disk type: local NVMe or network block storage.

outputs.name: Full vectors
outputs.meaning: Count × dimensions × 4 bytes: the size at full precision.

outputs.name: In-memory HNSW needs
outputs.meaning: Vectors plus graph links, all in RAM.

outputs.name: DiskANN RAM
outputs.meaning: PQ codes plus a fixed 16 GB for the cache and working memory.

outputs.name: SSD footprint
outputs.meaning: One or more 4 KB sectors per node, holding the full vector and neighbour IDs.

outputs.name: Round trips / reads
outputs.meaning: SSD round trips (L ÷ beam width) and sector reads per query.

outputs.name: Recall and latency
outputs.meaning: Modelled: they depend on L, code size, beam width and disk speed.

presets.name: 1 billion, short list
presets.expect: 3.07 TB of vectors; DiskANN needs 48.0 GB of RAM. L = 50 gives about 83% recall at 1.7 ms.

presets.name: Tuned list
presets.expect: L = 100: about 95% recall in 25 round trips, 2.9 ms on NVMe.

presets.name: 2 billion, big codes
presets.expect: 128-byte codes for 2 billion vectors need 272 GB of RAM: over budget.

presets.name: Network disk
presets.expect: The same index on network storage: about 96% recall but 20.4 ms per query.

missions.text: Serve 2 billion vectors within the 256 GB RAM budget at 95% recall or better.
missions.hint: 64-byte codes need 128 GB; raise L to 100.

missions.text: On local NVMe, reach 95% recall with latency at or under 5 ms.
missions.hint: From the start preset, raise L to 100.

missions.text: At 95% recall on NVMe, push latency above 5 ms by changing only the beam width.
missions.hint: A beam width of 1 turns every read into its own round trip.

practice.scenario: An image-search service holds 1 billion embeddings. Keeping them all in RAM would need about 3 TB; a DiskANN index on NVMe SSDs serves them from one large machine with tens of gigabytes of RAM.

industries.use: Billion-scale retrieval on far fewer machines
Years of documents without huge RAM bills

practice.analogy: A warehouse with a pocket catalogue. The catalogue in your pocket tells you which few shelves to visit, and only those boxes are pulled.

library.name: pgvectorscale or Milvus
library.what: pgvectorscale adds a StreamingDiskANN index to Postgres; Milvus offers a DISKANN index type for large clusters.

numericDrill.question: 500 million vectors × 768 float32 dimensions. How much RAM for 64-byte compressed codes instead of full vectors, in GB?
numericDrill.answer: Full vectors: 500M × 3,072 B ≈ 1.5 TB. Codes: 500M × 64 B = 32 GB in RAM, with the full vectors on SSD.

interview.question: How does DiskANN keep latency low while reading from SSD?
interview.answer: It navigates a graph in few hops using compressed vectors held in RAM, reads only a handful of SSD pages per query for full-precision vectors, and batches reads with beam search. Fast NVMe random reads make it practical.

interview.question: When is DiskANN the wrong choice?
interview.answer: At small or medium scale where vectors fit in RAM (HNSW is faster), on slow disks, or when the index changes constantly without a streaming or fresh variant.

mistakes.mistake: Running it on network or spinning disks
Benchmarking one query at a time
mistakes.fix: Measure p95 latency under concurrent load

quiz.question: An ads platform has 1 billion 768-dimension float32 vectors. How much space do the full vectors take?
quiz.explanation: 1 billion × 768 × 4 B ≈ 3.07 TB.

quiz.question: A marketplace stores 800 million listings as 32-byte PQ codes in RAM for DiskANN. How much RAM do the codes need?
quiz.explanation: 800 million × 32 B = 25.6 GB.

quiz.question: Which of these make DiskANN query latency worse? Select all that apply.
options: Network block storage instead of local NVMe
A beam width of 1 with a long candidate list
A warm cache of nodes near the entry point
Heavy concurrent load saturating the SSD
quiz.explanation: Slow reads, many sequential round trips and SSD queueing all add latency. A warm cache saves reads.

quiz.question: A DiskANN search uses a candidate list L = 120 and a beam width of 4. About how many SSD round trips does a query take?
quiz.explanation: ⌈120 ÷ 4⌉ = 30 round trips, each issuing up to 4 reads.

quiz.question: A radiology group has 20 million 512-dimension vectors (about 41 GB) on a server with 128 GB of RAM. Which index fits best?
quiz.explanation: 20 million × 2,048 B ≈ 41 GB fits in RAM with room for links, and in-memory HNSW is faster than SSD reads.

quiz.question: Why does DiskANN store each node’s full vector in the same SSD sector as its neighbour list?
options: One read gives both the next hops and the exact distance for the final re-rank
It frees the SSD for other data
quiz.explanation: The walk needs the neighbour list anyway, so the full vector comes free for exact re-ranking.

quiz.question: During a DiskANN search, what decides which nodes to read next?
options: Exact distances from full vectors held in RAM
Approximate distances from the PQ codes held in RAM
quiz.explanation: Compressed codes in RAM guide the walk. Full vectors are read from SSD only for the visited nodes.

quiz.question: Each DiskANN node stores its 1,536-dimension float32 vector plus 64 neighbour IDs of 4 bytes and a 4-byte count. How many 4 KB sectors does a node need?
Which of these are DiskANN-based options? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: pgvectorscale, Milvus and FreshDiskANN all build on DiskANN. hnswlib implements HNSW.

quiz.question: A DiskANN index has recall 0.92 against a 0.95 target, with latency to spare. What do you change?
options: Raise the candidate list size L
quiz.explanation: A longer candidate list explores more of the graph and raises recall, at the cost of more reads.

quiz.question: A shop has 1 million product vectors and RAM to spare. How does DiskANN compare with in-memory HNSW here?
options: In-memory HNSW is usually faster, because nothing waits on SSD reads
quiz.explanation: DiskANN pays off when data exceeds RAM. At small scale, SSD reads only add latency.

quiz.question: PQ code size is raised from 32 to 64 bytes. Which of these happen? Select all that apply.
options: Recall improves at the same candidate list size
Distances that guide the walk become more accurate
quiz.explanation: Finer codes guide the search better and double RAM. The full vectors on SSD are unchanged.

quiz.question: Why benchmark DiskANN p95 latency under concurrent load rather than one query at a time?
options: SSD queues build up under concurrency, so single-query tests understate real latency
quiz.explanation: Many queries share the same device, and queueing on random reads shows up only under load.

quiz.question: A bank has 2 billion 768-dimension vectors and 256 GB of RAM. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: The full vectors take about 6.1 TB
32-byte PQ codes take 64 GB of RAM
In-memory HNSW would fit in 256 GB
128-byte codes alone would take all 256 GB
quiz.explanation: 2 billion × 3,072 B ≈ 6.1 TB; × 32 B = 64 GB; × 128 B = 256 GB. Full vectors cannot fit in RAM.

quiz.question: With L = 100, raising the beam width from 4 to 8 changes the round trips from 25 to about how many?
quiz.explanation: ⌈100 ÷ 8⌉ = ⌈12.5⌉ = 13 round trips, with more reads per trip.

quiz.question: An archive plans to index 3 billion documents with DiskANN. What should the plan account for?
options: Builds at this scale take many hours and a lot of memory, so schedule rebuilds
The index is rebuilt per query
quiz.explanation: Very large graph builds are slow and memory-hungry, which matters for rebuild schedules.

quiz.question: Listings change thousands of times an hour in a DiskANN-backed search. What should you use?
options: A static DiskANN index rebuilt after every insert
A streaming variant such as FreshDiskANN, or StreamingDiskANN in pgvectorscale
quiz.explanation: Streaming variants accept inserts and deletes without full rebuilds.

quiz.question: An airline stores 500 million vectors as 64-byte PQ codes and reserves 16 GB for cache and working memory. How much RAM does DiskANN need?
quiz.explanation: 500 million × 64 B = 32 GB of codes, plus 16 GB = 48 GB.

quiz.question: Which conditions matter for good DiskANN performance? Select all that apply.
options: Local NVMe SSDs with fast random reads
Enough RAM for the PQ codes
A tuned candidate list and beam width
All full vectors held in RAM
quiz.explanation: DiskANN is designed so that full vectors stay on SSD. Fast disks, RAM for codes and tuning matter.

quiz.question: A payments firm on Postgres has 150 million vectors and wants to stay in Postgres. Which tool fits?
quiz.explanation: pgvectorscale adds a DiskANN-style index to Postgres for datasets beyond comfortable RAM.
